etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Ancient Greek κεραμικός (keramikós, “potter's”), from κέραμος (kéramos, “potter's clay”), perhaps from a pre-Hellenic word or from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₂- (“to heat, burn, fire”).

definitions.definition: Made of material produced by the high-temperature firing of inorganic, nonmetallic rocks and minerals.

quote.citation: 2021 April 5, Jessica Bumpus, “Ceramics Are in Fashion”, in The New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: And over the past year, a new crop of collaborations between designers and artists has turned a spotlight on ceramic sculptures characterized by organic and biomorphic forms.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A hard, brittle, inorganic, nonmetallic material, usually made from a material, such as clay, then firing it at a high temperature.
(countable) An object made of this material.

quote.citation: 2021 April 5, Jessica Bumpus, “Ceramics Are in Fashion”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: Photographed by Juergen Teller, the project included a series of JW Anderson women’s wear looks, still-life images and sketches of Ms. Odundo and Ms. Corbett’s ceramics, as well as their portraits, and blankets designed as part of the collaboration.
